reference.source: Kelley & Firestein's Textbook of Rheumatology / EULAR systemic sclerosis guidance
clinicalPearls: Patients have the internal organ and vascular features of systemic sclerosis without clinically detectable skin thickening
Raynaud phenomenon, a scleroderma-pattern nailfold capillary picture, and systemic sclerosis-specific autoantibodies support the diagnosis
Interstitial lung disease, pulmonary arterial hypertension, oesophageal dysmotility, or renal crisis may still occur
The absence of skin change frequently delays recognition until an internal organ complication declares itself
Autoantibody profiles resemble those of cutaneous systemic sclerosis, including anticentromere and anti-topoisomerase I patterns
Organ-based surveillance mirrors that used in cutaneous systemic sclerosis despite normal skin
It should be considered in unexplained pulmonary hypertension or interstitial lung disease with Raynaud
reference.pathophysiology: Systemic sclerosis sine scleroderma shares the immune activation, small-vessel vasculopathy, and internal fibrosis of cutaneous systemic sclerosis but without the dermal fibrosis that produces visible skin thickening. Endothelial injury, autoantibody production, and profibrotic signalling target the lungs, gastrointestinal tract, heart, and kidneys while sparing the skin clinically. The same pathogenic mechanisms therefore generate pulmonary vascular disease, interstitial fibrosis, and dysmotility, meaning the visceral risk profile parallels that of overt scleroderma.
additionalInvestigations: Antinuclear antibody with systemic sclerosis-specific antibody profiling
High-resolution CT and pulmonary function tests for interstitial lung disease
Transthoracic echocardiography screening for pulmonary hypertension
Oesophageal function studies when dysmotility is suspected
Renal function and blood pressure monitoring
redFlags: Unexplained progressive breathlessness from pulmonary vascular or interstitial disease
Hypertensive crisis with rising creatinine suggesting renal crisis
reference.prognosis: Outcome depends on the specific internal organ involvement; the visceral complications carry the same risks as in cutaneous disease, and pulmonary vascular or interstitial disease dominates prognosis. Early recognition despite normal skin allows timely organ-directed treatment.
pitfalls: Excluding systemic sclerosis simply because the skin is normal
Labelling pulmonary hypertension as idiopathic without checking autoantibodies and capillaroscopy
Delaying surveillance for internal organ disease
Overlooking the risk of renal crisis in the absence of skin change
references: EULAR recommendations for the treatment of systemic sclerosis
management: Vasodilator therapy for Raynaud phenomenon and digital ischaemia with calcium channel blockers and phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors
Immunosuppression and antifibrotic therapy (mycophenolate, cyclophosphamide, rituximab, nintedanib) for interstitial lung disease
Targeted pulmonary vasodilators for pulmonary arterial hypertension confirmed on right heart catheterisation
Proton pump inhibitors and prokinetics for oesophageal and gastrointestinal dysmotility
ACE-inhibitor therapy for scleroderma renal crisis, with avoidance of high-dose corticosteroids
Organ-based surveillance mirroring cutaneous disease, with pulmonary function tests, echocardiography, and blood pressure and renal monitoring despite normal skin
Multidisciplinary specialist follow-up to enable early detection of visceral complications
